changes.before: Complete takeRequest(state, now). State has windowStart and count. Within each 1000-unit time window, allow at most 3 requests. At now >= windowStart + 1000 start a new window at now. Return {allowed,state} without mutating the input. Times are nondecreasing and supplied in the same units.
changes.after: A rate limit lets through only a set number of requests in a time window.

before: A rate limit restricts how many requests may be accepted during a stated interval.
A fixed-duration window keeps its start time and the number accepted so far.
Check expiration before checking the count. At the exact end boundary, the next window may begin.
For this exercise, three requests fit each 1000-unit window. The fourth is rejected until a new window begins.
Return a new state object so the caller can retain the previous snapshot.
A real HTTP server can report an exceeded limit with 429 Too Many Requests. Its policy may also explain when retrying is allowed.
The provided clock is monotonic for this exercise. Real designs must handle clock behavior, user identity, shared storage, and requests reaching several servers.
This is one policy model, not a complete abuse-prevention system. Test just before and exactly at the reset boundary.
after: A rate limit controls how many requests can pass during a set time. Our rule allows three requests per window.
A window is one span of time. Store its start in windowStart and the number of accepted requests in count.
The window ends when now >= windowStart + 1000. Check this first. When it ends, start a window at now with count 0.
Complete takeRequest(state, now). Return {allowed, state} with a new state object. Accept and count a request only if fewer than three have passed in its window.
When a real HTTP server rejects a request for exceeding a rate limit, it can return status 429: Too Many Requests.
The supplied times use the same units and never go backward. A count only makes sense when every time uses the same clock rules.
Test the fourth request before the window ends, then another exactly at the end. The first is blocked. The second starts the new window with count 1.

before.question: The window began at 50 and lasts 1000 units. The count is already 3. At time 1050, should the next request be allowed?
choices: Yes; the exact boundary starts a new window before the count check.
No; the old count blocks forever.
Only if the request changes its clock units.
before.explanation: 1050 equals 50 + 1000. Under this policy the previous window has ended, so the new request begins a fresh count.

after.question: A window starts at 50 and lasts 1000 units. Its count is 3. Is a request at time 1050 allowed?
choices: Yes. A new window starts before checking the count.
No. The old count blocks every future request.
Only after changing the clock units.
after.explanation: 1050 is exactly 50 + 1000. The old window has ended. The new request becomes the first in the new window.

changes.before: No real request traffic is limited. This in-memory state transition uses a supplied clock; production enforcement needs an explicit identity/keying and distributed consistency policy.
changes.after: This browser exercise models one limit with a supplied clock. It does not limit real network traffic. A real service must decide whose requests share a limit and keep the count consistent across its servers.

project.title: Allow only three requests per window
project.task: Complete takeRequest(state, now). Allow at most 3 requests per 1000-unit window. At now >= windowStart + 1000, start a new window at now. Return {allowed,state} without changing the input. Supplied times never decrease and use the same units.
